blocks.text: To use the same algorithm with different types you write it **generic**. The type parameter goes in square brackets: `[T]`. `T: Ord` is a **bound**: `T` must be an orderable (`<`, `>`) type. At the call the type is usually inferred; you can also write it out, `larger[i64](...)`.

code: fn larger[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T:

blocks.text: For every combination of types the compiler produces code specialised and optimised for that type (like C++ templates). There is no extra run-time cost, boxing or type erasure.

blocks.prompt: Write `smaller[T: Ord](a, b)`: it returns the smaller one. Print `smaller(7, 3)` and `smaller(2.5, 9.5)`.
solution: fn smaller[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T:
blocks.hint: Start with `fn smaller[T: Ord](a: T, b: T) -> T:`.

blocks.q: Is a generic function slower at run time?
options: Yes, the type is looked up on every call
No, separate code is compiled for each type
blocks.why: The type is resolved at compile time (monomorphization).
